clue.text: Holy man supplied female with a drink

parts.note: kir is a French aperitif of white wine and blackcurrant liqueur

explanation.surface: A holy man was handed a drink by a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A fakir is a Muslim or Hindu religious ascetic who lives on alms, a holy man.

clue.text: Andy Capp's wife's entertaining the troops — and how! — in this?

definitions.text: Andy Capp's wife's entertaining the troops — and how! — in this?

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to hold them within one's home, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: Flo is the wife in the long-running British newspaper cartoon strip Andy Capp; with the possessive she gives FLOS
OR stands for other ranks, the ordinary soldiers
taken as written

explanation.surface: A comic-strip wife is putting on a cabaret for the soldiers, and what a show it is.
explanation.walkthrough: Unusually the possessive 's is counted as a letter after the wife's name. Andy Capp is a British newspaper cartoon about a work-shy northern man and his long-suffering wife.
explanation.definitionFit: A floor show is a cabaret performed on the floor of a club, the sort of thing staged to entertain troops.

clue.text: Stores' takings finally look up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word look is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to peek is to take a quick look

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word takings

explanation.surface: A shop's end-of-day takings are finally looking healthier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns PEEK into KEEP, and 'finally' gives S, the last letter of 'takings'. The definition is the verb: someone keeps or stores things.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep supplies is to store them, so the verb form matches with its third-person ending.

clue.text: Confine wild critters

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of the next word running loose in a new order

explanation.surface: Keep untamed animals locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' signals an anagram of CRITTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrict someone is to keep them within limits, to confine them.

clue.text: Loans sufficient for small part of population

parts.note: subs are advance payments or small loans, as in subbing a friend
ample means enough, sufficient

explanation.surface: Lending enough to cover a fraction of the people.
explanation.walkthrough: SUBS is British informal for small loans or advances against wages.
explanation.definitionFit: A subsample is a smaller sample drawn from a larger sample of a statistical population.

clue.text: Feature of herb garden: saxifrage borders?

indicators.note: only the borders of the word saxifrage are kept, its two letters at each edge, with the middle dropped

explanation.surface: A gardener wonders whether saxifrage edges a herb bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'borders' keeps the first two and last two letters of SAXIFRAGE, dropping XIFRA. The surface makes 'borders' look like flower beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage is a common culinary herb, an obvious plant in any herb garden.

clue.text: Ice cream container, perhaps, turned upside down and held securely

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upside down means the whole phrase reads from bottom to top

parts.note: an ice cream tub is one kind of dessert tub, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: A tub of ice cream is flipped over and held firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned upside down' reverses DESSERT TUB letter by letter, giving BUT TRESSED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something buttressed is propped up and supported, so held securely in place.

clue.text: Earnest request a PM once expressed in words

indicators.note: spoken words, so the phrase before is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a British Prime Minister in the 1830s and 1840s, so 'a PM once' is A PEEL

explanation.surface: A former prime minister put a heartfelt plea into words.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Peel, founder of the modern police, was twice British Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: An appeal is a serious or urgent request for help or support.

clue.text: First-time mother is prudish with one soldier that's dropped in

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper, prudish
I is the Roman numeral one
a para is a paratrooper, a soldier dropped by parachute

explanation.surface: A new mother is strait-laced, and a paratrooper has dropped in to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is only a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Primipara is the medical term for a woman giving birth for the first time.

clue.text: Lament English support coming to end in Germany

parts.note: a leg supports a table or chair

indicators.note: the end in a word is its final letter, here of Germany

explanation.surface: An English backer arrives at the finish in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end in' gives Y, the last letter of 'Germany'; 'coming to' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem, a lament for the dead.

clue.text: To emit sad sound in public is a mistake

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other

parts.note: overt means open, done in public
to sigh is to let out a sad sound

explanation.surface: Sighing openly is an error of manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To emit sad sound' is a verb phrase standing for its one-word synonym, and 'in' does the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: An oversight is an error caused by failing to notice something, a mistake.

clue.text: Force tiniest possible wage increase?

parts.note: the penny, abbreviated P, is the smallest British coin
a rise is the British word for a pay increase

explanation.surface: A tiny pay rise is all a boss can be made to give.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'p rise' would be a one-penny raise, the smallest possible.
explanation.definitionFit: To prise something open is to force it, usually with a lever.

clue.text: Metro's trains too long for platforms

indicators.note: the phrase is longer than needed, so only a run of letters inside it gives the answer

explanation.surface: Underground trains are too long for the station platforms.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits inside metRO'S TRAins; the surface has a familiar commuting gripe.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostra is a plural of rostrum, a raised platform for a speaker.

clue.text: Fashion bra worn by one showing sophistication

indicators.note: a garment worn by someone sits around them, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: unity is the quality of being one

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so the letters of bra are reshaped

explanation.surface: A stylish bra worn by someone shows how refined they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' gives RBA, which 'worn by' places inside the word for oneness.
explanation.definitionFit: Urbanity is suave refinement of manner, a synonym for sophistication.

clue.text: Collapsed suddenly in university town

parts.note: Keele is an English university, in Staffordshire
Dover is a Kent port town

explanation.surface: Someone fainted in a college town.
explanation.walkthrough: Keele is a campus university in Staffordshire, and Dover is the Channel port in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: To keel over is to fall down suddenly, as a ship capsizes.

clue.text: Too bad he searched in vain

indicators.note: a futile search scatters things everywhere, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: He searched with no luck, and nobody sympathises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in vain' signals an anagram of HE SEARCHED.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard cheese is a British idiom meaning bad luck, often said without much sympathy.

clue.text: On-stream, seen frequently

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in letters
a current is a flowing stream

explanation.surface: A broadcast on-stream is seen often.
explanation.definitionFit: Recurrent means happening repeatedly, so something recurrent is seen frequently.

clue.text: Preserve second-class post

parts.note: jam is a fruit preserve
B is the grade below A, second class

explanation.surface: A jar of preserves sent by second-class mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' looks like mail but is an upright.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamb is the vertical post forming the side of a door or window frame.

clue.text: Cover several courses under heading of "Education degree"

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece comes underneath another that heads it

parts.note: BEd is a Bachelor of Education degree
a spread is a large meal of many dishes

explanation.surface: A college covers several courses for an education degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under heading of' puts SPREAD beneath BED.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedspread is a decorative cover laid over a bed.

clue.text: Increasing size of one room in part of building

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other

parts.note: a wing is a section projecting from a main building
I is the Roman numeral one
a den is a small private room

explanation.surface: A single room in one wing of a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does the containing; 'of' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Widening means growing broader, increasing in size.

clue.text: Week touring endlessly cold Scottish town

indicators.note: a tour goes around, so one piece wraps around the other
the word loses its last letter

parts.note: icy means very cold

explanation.surface: A week travelling round a chilly town in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' leaves IC, and 'touring' wraps the abbreviation for week around it. Wick is a town in the far north of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Wick is a town in Caithness in northern Scotland.

clue.text: Top sportsman, foremost among rugby's international players, gets trophy

parts.note: a blue is someone who has represented Oxford or Cambridge University at sport

indicators.note: foremost means the first letter, here of rugby's

parts.note: a band is a group of musicians, players

explanation.surface: An elite athlete, leading a rugby side's internationals, collects a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: A Blue is an award given to a top sportsman at Oxford or Cambridge. 'foremost among' gives R from 'rugby's'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Blue Riband is a trophy for the fastest Atlantic crossing, and by extension any top prize.

clue.text: Villain ordered to hold up proof of identity

indicators.note: holding something keeps it inside, so one piece goes in the other

parts.note: bade is the past tense of bid, ordered

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: ID is short for identification

explanation.surface: A crook is told to produce some ID.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' gives DI, and 'to hold' places it inside the past tense of bid.
explanation.definitionFit: A baddie is informal for a villain, the bad guy in a story.

clue.text: Bit of cloth pulled back secures flower arrangements

indicators.note: pulling back sends the word the other way, read backwards

parts.note: a rag is a scrap of cloth
to land a deal is to secure it

explanation.surface: Drawing back a cloth reveals displays of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulled back' turns RAG into GAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Garlands are wreaths of flowers woven together, a kind of floral arrangement.

clue.text: Shylock's man heads for gondola, or boat behind one

indicators.note: the heads of the following words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A Venetian servant makes for a gondola, or a boat following one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads for' takes the first letters of 'gondola, or boat behind one'. Launcelot Gobbo is Shylock's servant in The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Launcelot Gobbo is the clown who serves Shylock in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: At start of banquet, empty what's in dish and mug

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, here of banquet

parts.note: to eat up is to finish everything on the plate

explanation.surface: At a feast, clear your plate and your cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mug' looks like a cup but is the verb meaning to attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug someone is to attack and rob them, to beat them up.

clue.text: Opponent disheartened after he is dismissed from the test

indicators.note: one piece is placed after the other
the following word loses the letters named before
the heart of the word, its middle letter, is removed

parts.note: a rival is an opponent

explanation.surface: A cricketer's opponent is downcast after he is out in the Test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is dismissed from' leaves T; 'disheartened' gives the currency word, which comes 'after' it. The surface suggests a cricket Test match.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial is a test of quality or performance.

clue.text: One-time novelist was one

parts.note: a novelist of former times, Sir Walter of Ivanhoe and Waverley, belonged to this nation; dropping one T, for time, from his surname also leads there

explanation.surface: A novelist of old was one of a kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Walter Scott was born in Edinburgh; 'One-time' also hints at removing one T from his name.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Scotland, as Sir Walter Scott was, is described by this word.

clue.text: Money raised by speech

indicators.note: spoken words, so the word before is heard not spelt

parts.note: bred means raised, as children or livestock

explanation.surface: Funds raised through a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' looks like fundraising but means brought up.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money.

clue.text: Bully boy is into wicked behaviour

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other

parts.note: vice is immoral behaviour
Tim is a boy's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boy is getting into bad ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' does the containing; 'Bully' is the verb, not the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To victimise someone is to single them out for unfair treatment, to bully them.

clue.text: One after another, any number will tuck into fresh hot roly-poly dessert

indicators.note: to tuck into is to go inside, so one piece enters another
fresh means made anew, so the letters of hot are rearranged

parts.note: N stands for an unspecified number in maths

indicators.note: roly-poly suggests rolling about, so the letters are tumbled

parts.note: a torte is a rich cake served as a dessert

explanation.surface: Someone tucks greedily into a hot jam roly-poly pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' gives OTH, 'will tuck into' puts the number inside it, and 'roly-poly' gives ETROT. Jam roly-poly is a British rolled suet pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: On the trot is British idiom for in succession, one after another.

clue.text: Cold and served in aspic, say

indicators.note: say signals the word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: food served in aspic is jellied, as with jellied eels

explanation.surface: A dish served chilled and set in savoury jelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelid means icy cold, from the Latin for frost.
